structure.title: Table of Contents
structure.summary: This partial document outlines the architecture and main components of a data integration platform. It covers the types of data being integrated, the connector framework (including types, roadmap, and authentication), and the field mapping engine with schema and mapping processes. It details data transformation and normalization steps, sync management (including scheduling and error handling), and the routing of data to different platform targets. The document also discusses outbound data write-back processes, provides an end-to-end data pipeline flow with code, and describes relevant database schemas. Additional sections address CSV import flows, nuances and risks, and summarize key technical decisions.

structure.title: Module 4: Data Integration Layer
structure.prefix_summary: The partial document outlines the purpose and architecture of the Data Integration Layer, which connects tenants' business systems (such as CRMs, ERPs, and spreadsheets) to the platform. It details how the layer extracts, maps, normalizes, deduplicates, and enriches data before delivering it to core platform components. The document explains the MVP approach, which relies solely on CSV/Excel imports to avoid complex engineering work associated with live CRM connectors, and notes that connectors (like Salesforce and HubSpot) are planned for future phases. The architecture is designed for easy integration of connectors without changes to the data processing pipeline.

nodes.title: 4.1 What Data Are We Integrating?
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the types of data integrated by Module 4 of a platform, detailing both inbound and outbound data flows. It outlines four main inbound data categories: Account/Customer Data (company and account details from CRM systems), Contact Data (stakeholder information from CRM), Product/Purchase Data (customer product ownership and transaction history from CRM and ERP), and KB Content Data (product catalog and related documents). Each category specifies its contents, source systems, destination within the platform, and the business rationale for its integration. Additionally, it covers outbound data—specifically, AI-generated activities and opportunities written back to CRM systems—emphasizing the importance of closing the feedback loop for sales and pipeline tracking. The document highlights how these data integrations enable personalized interactions, informed recommendations, and comprehensive CRM records.

nodes.title: 4.2 Connector Framework
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 4.2 Connector Framework

Each external system connects through a connector — a standardized adapter that handles authentication, API protocols, pagination, rate limiting, and data extraction. Connectors are pluggable: adding a new CRM means writing a new connector, not changing anything downstream.

nodes.title: 4.2.1 Connector Types and Roadmap
nodes.summary: This partial document outlines the types of data connectors planned for integration, detailing their authentication methods, data extraction approaches, support for incremental synchronization, and their prioritization in the development roadmap. It lists connectors such as CSV/Excel Upload (included in the MVP), Salesforce, HubSpot, Dynamics 365, NetSuite, SAP, and a Generic REST API, specifying for each the authentication protocol (e.g., OAuth, API Key), data pull method (e.g., REST API, file parsing), incremental sync strategy (e.g., polling, webhooks), and the phase in which they will be implemented (MVP, Phase 2, or Phase 3). The table helps prioritize connector development and clarifies technical requirements for each integration.

nodes.title: 4.2.2 Connector Interface Contract
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the standardized interface contract that all data connectors must implement within the system. It outlines an abstract base class, BaseConnector, which defines required asynchronous methods for authentication, initial data loading, incremental synchronization, writing data back to the source, and retrieving the source schema. The document provides a concrete example implementation, CsvConnector, which handles CSV and Excel file uploads, detailing how it authenticates (no authentication needed), loads data (using pandas to parse files and yield records), and handles incremental sync (by re-uploading files). The main point emphasized is that all connectors, regardless of the data source (e.g., CSV files or APIs like Salesforce), output data in a unified RawRecord format, enabling downstream processes to be agnostic to the data source.

nodes.title: 4.2.3 Auth and Credential Store
nodes.summary: This partial document section outlines the authentication and credential storage strategy for CRM connectors in a multi-tenant environment. It describes an OAuth Token Manager that manages the OAuth 2.0 flow per tenant, ensuring tokens are isolated and securely handled. Credentials, including OAuth tokens, API keys, and basic auth details, are encrypted at rest using Azure Key Vault or AES-256, and never stored in plaintext. The system includes a background job to proactively refresh tokens before expiry and notifies admins if re-authorization is needed. However, for the MVP (Minimum Viable Product), OAuth authentication is not implemented; instead, data is ingested via CSV uploads to avoid the complexity and engineering effort of OAuth integration for each CRM.

nodes.title: 4.3 Field Mapping Engine
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 4.3 Field Mapping Engine

| Why Field Mapping Exists Every CRM and every CSV uses different field names. Salesforce calls it ‘Account.Industry’, HubSpot calls it ‘company.industry_type’, a CSV column might say ‘cust_industry’ or ‘Customer Industry’ or ‘INDUSTRY_CODE’. Our platform needs a consistent internal schema. The Field Mapper translates any tenant’s field names to our canonical platform fields. Without this layer, every downstream module would need to handle N different schemas. |
| --- |

nodes.title: 4.3.1 Platform Canonical Schema
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the "Platform Canonical Schema," which is the standardized internal data model that all data connectors must map into, regardless of the original data source. It provides a detailed table outlining the canonical fields for three main objects: Account, Contact, and Transaction. For each object, the schema specifies field names, data types, whether the field is required, and a brief description of its purpose. Key fields include identifiers for deduplication and synchronization, company and contact details, normalized classifications (such as industry and lifecycle stage), and transaction information (such as product SKU, amount, and date). The schema ensures consistent data structure across different integrations, facilitating reliable data processing and analysis within the platform.

nodes.title: 4.3.2 The Mapping Process
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the field mapping process in a data integration pipeline. It outlines the steps taken before data transformation and normalization, starting with source schema discovery (identifying available fields from sources like CSV headers or Salesforce metadata). The system then auto-suggests field mappings using techniques such as name similarity, data pattern matching, sample value analysis, and data type inference. An admin reviews and confirms these mappings via a UI, with required fields flagged if unmapped. Confirmed mappings are saved in a PostgreSQL table as tenant-specific configurations, ensuring mappings are reused for future data syncs. The document also provides the schema for the field mapping configuration table and example entries, illustrating how source fields are linked to canonical fields and how optional transformation rules can be applied.

nodes.title: 4.3.3 Auto-Suggest — ML-Based Field Matching
nodes.summary: This partial document section discusses the design and implementation plan for an ML-based auto-suggest feature for field matching during data onboarding. It outlines that auto-suggest is intended for the full product, not the MVP, where field mapping will be done manually for each tenant. The document details the auto-suggest scoring model, which combines signals such as column name similarity, data pattern matching, value set matching, and positional heuristics, each with assigned weights. It explains how each signal works with examples and describes the confidence threshold for auto-suggestions in the UI. The section concludes with a decision rationale: auto-suggest will be developed later when onboarding scales, as it requires additional infrastructure and is not needed for initial manual setups.

nodes.title: 4.4 Transform & Normalize
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 4.4 Transform & Normalize

After field mapping, data enters the transform pipeline. This is where messy, inconsistent real-world data becomes clean, uniform, enriched records ready for the platform.

nodes.title: 4.4.1 Data Normalizer
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the "Data Normalizer" component, which standardizes data fields from various source systems into consistent formats. It outlines normalization rules for different field types, including dates, currency, industry and segment enums, phone numbers, email addresses, boolean values, null values, and company names. The document provides specific input variations, normalized outputs, and the rules or libraries used for each field type. It emphasizes tenant-specific configurability, allowing for custom synonym maps and normalization logic based on tenant requirements, with configurations stored in a dedicated database column. The goal is to ensure data consistency and accuracy across diverse data sources.

nodes.title: 4.4.2 Deduplication
nodes.summary: This partial document section describes the deduplication process for imported data, focusing on how duplicate records representing the same real-world entity (such as accounts, contacts, or products) are detected and merged before being committed to the platform database. It outlines a three-tier matching strategy: (1) exact match on external IDs (e.g., Salesforce or HubSpot IDs), (2) deterministic match on business keys (such as domain, email, or SKU), and (3) configurable fuzzy matching using string similarity and secondary signals (like city or revenue range). The document details the merge strategy for confirmed duplicates, specifying rules for scalar fields, arrays, financial values, and platform-generated data, and emphasizes maintaining an audit trail for all merges. It also includes a code snippet illustrating the deduplication logic and notes that, for the MVP (minimum viable product), only exact and deterministic matches are enabled by default, with fuzzy matching available as a configurable option for future releases. The rationale for this decision is to avoid the risks of incorrect merges due to untuned fuzzy matching, especially since MVP data imports are expected to be cleaner.

nodes.title: 4.4.3 Data Enricher
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the "Data Enricher" component, which is responsible for adding computed fields to account data that are not present in the original source but are essential for enhancing agent intelligence and automation. It provides a detailed table listing each computed field, the logic or formula used to derive it, where it is stored (primarily in the account_enrichment table), and which agents or system components utilize the field. The computed fields include metrics such as total lifetime value, products owned count, categories owned, whitespace percentage, months since last purchase, average deal size, purchase frequency, year-over-year revenue growth, computed segment, account health score, cross-sell opportunity count, and contract expiry days. The enrichment process is described as a batch job that recalculates these fields for all accounts after every data sync, ensuring data consistency and idempotency. The enriched data supports various use cases, including account sizing, cross-sell and upsell opportunities, win-back strategies, account health monitoring, and renewal management.

nodes.title: 4.4.4 Aggregations
nodes.summary:
This partial document section discusses the implementation of data aggregations for business intelligence, focusing on generating insights at both the segment and tenant levels. It covers:

- Segment-level benchmarks, such as average products owned by customers in specific industries or segments, to contextualize recommendations for agents.
- Tenant-level statistics, including average product count, median deal size, and top product categories, used for dashboards and analytics.
- Time-series aggregations, like monthly revenue and seasonal purchase patterns, to support trend detection and renewal strategies.
- Product popularity rankings, identifying top-selling and fastest-growing products for recommendation purposes.
- The structure and periodic recomputation of the segment_benchmarks database table, which stores aggregated metrics for each tenant, industry, and segment.

nodes.title: 4.5.1 Initial Load
nodes.summary: This partial document section describes the "Initial Load" process when a tenant first connects their data source. It explains that the initial load is a one-time, bulk import of all historical data, which is necessary to establish a comprehensive baseline for analytics, particularly for co-occurrence analysis in the Product Graph Layer. The process differs by data source: for CSV uploads, the entire file is loaded; for CRM connectors, all historical records (accounts, contacts, opportunities, transactions) are imported, potentially covering several years and large data volumes. The document emphasizes the importance of full historical data for reliable pattern detection, outlines technical requirements for the initial load (pagination, resumability, idempotency), and details where different types of data are stored and which system components read them. It also clarifies that the initial load is only performed once, with subsequent updates handled by incremental syncs, except when a new CSV is uploaded, which triggers a full replacement.

nodes.title: 4.5.2 Incremental Sync
nodes.summary: This partial document section explains the concept and implementation of incremental synchronization (incremental sync) for CRM data integration. It describes two main mechanisms for detecting and retrieving changed records after the initial data load: polling (where the system periodically requests records modified since the last sync timestamp) and webhooks (where the CRM pushes change events in near-real-time). The document details how sync cursors (timestamps) are tracked per tenant and object type to ensure only new or updated records are processed. It lists the types of changes that trigger a sync (such as updates to accounts, contacts, transactions, and products) and clarifies that the system pulls entire records when any change is detected, rather than tracking individual field changes. Additionally, it provides a database schema for tracking sync cursor state and sync outcomes.

nodes.title: 4.5.3 Scheduler
nodes.summary: This partial document section describes the scheduler component responsible for determining when synchronization (sync) operations are executed. It outlines three main scheduling functions: (1) Polling schedule, which configures how often data is polled from external systems (e.g., Salesforce) for updates, with customizable intervals per tenant and object type; (2) Batch recomputation schedule, which triggers downstream processing jobs (such as analytics or enrichment) after syncs or at regular intervals; and (3) Full reconciliation schedule, which periodically performs comprehensive data consistency checks to correct any discrepancies between systems. The section also includes a database schema for configuring sync schedules, specifying fields such as tenant ID, connector type, object type, sync method, polling interval, cron expressions for batch jobs, and status tracking.

nodes.title: 4.5.4 Retry and Error Handling — Dead Letter Queue
nodes.summary: The partial document describes the retry and error handling mechanism for data synchronization using a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ). It explains that individual record failures during processing (such as mapping, normalization, deduplication, or enrichment errors) are isolated and sent to the DLQ, preventing them from blocking the processing of other records in the batch. The DLQ stores details about failed records, including the raw data, error message, failed step, attempt count, and timestamps. A background job periodically retries DLQ records, handling transient errors automatically and escalating permanent failures after a configurable number of attempts. Administrators are alerted to unresolved records and can review, fix, skip, or adjust processing rules. The document also provides a database schema for the DLQ table, detailing its fields and structure.

nodes.title: 4.6 Platform Targets — Where Data Goes
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 4.6 Platform Targets — Where Data Goes

After processing, clean data is delivered to two platform modules:

nodes.title: 4.6.1 State Engine (Module 1)
nodes.summary: This partial document describes the "State Engine" (Module 1), which is responsible for managing and delivering key account context information to agents during customer interactions. It outlines the types of data stored in the session state, including account profiles, contact records, current product ownership, enrichment data, and account owner mapping. The document explains where each type of information is located within the session state and provides examples of how agents and automated tools use this data to personalize conversations, generate emails, identify cross-sell and upsell opportunities, assess account value, and verify account ownership.

nodes.title: 4.6.2 KB Engine (Module 3)
nodes.summary:
### 4.6.2 KB Engine (Module 3)

The KB Engine receives product and purchase data:

| What Gets Delivered | KB Engine Location | How It’s Used |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product catalog (SKUs, names, descriptions, categories, pricing, features) | PostgreSQL: products table + Foundry IQ product-descriptions knowledge source | Direct product lookup by SKU/category. Semantic search for product matching. Agent recommendations reference specific products. |
| Transaction history (full purchase records) | PostgreSQL: transactions table → Product Graph Layer 1 builder | Co-occurrence analysis: 'Products frequently bought together.' Sequential pattern mining. Upgrade detection. This is the raw material for the Product Relationship Graph. |
| Account-product mapping (current ownership per account) | PostgreSQL: account_products materialized view | Graph traversal starts from owned products: 'Given they have Product A, what should they also have?' |

nodes.title: 4.7 Outbound — Write-Back Service (Full Product)
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 4.7 Outbound — Write-Back Service (Full Product)

| Full Product Only Write-back to CRM is NOT in MVP. In MVP, recommendations and conversations exist only within our platform. The rep can manually create opportunities in their CRM based on AI recommendations. Write-back is Phase 2 and depends on having CRM connectors established (which are also Phase 2). |
| --- |

nodes.title: 4.7.1 What Gets Written Back
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the types of data written back to CRM systems (like Salesforce or HubSpot) following AI-driven sales recommendations. It details four main write-back actions: creating new opportunities or deals when a rep accepts a recommendation, logging activities for each AI conversation session, updating account fields with AI-enriched values (if configured), and creating follow-up tasks based on AI suggestions. For each action, the document specifies when it is triggered, what records are created in the CRM, and which fields are populated, including contextual information such as linked accounts, recommended products, estimated values, conversation summaries, custom AI scores, and follow-up details.

nodes.title: 4.7.2 Outbound Field Mapping
nodes.summary: This partial document section discusses outbound field mapping for CRM integrations, specifically focusing on how internal system fields are mapped back to the corresponding fields in external CRMs like Salesforce and HubSpot during write-back operations. It provides a concrete example of field mappings for both Salesforce’s Opportunity object and HubSpot’s Deal object, highlighting differences in field names and the need for custom fields (e.g., AI_Rec_ID__c in Salesforce). The document explains that outbound mapping is configured during the CRM connector setup phase, where administrators define which CRM fields should be updated. It also notes that any required custom fields must be created in the CRM by the tenant’s administrator before mapping.

nodes.title: 4.7.3 Write-Back Safety
nodes.summary:
### 4.7.3 Write-Back Safety

Writing to a tenant’s CRM is a high-stakes operation. Safeguards:

Explicit confirmation required: Write-back never happens automatically. The rep must click ‘Create in CRM’ and confirm. No background auto-creation of opportunities.

Idempotent writes: If the write fails and retries, it must not create duplicate opportunities. Every write-back record includes our internal recommendation_id. Before creating, check if an opportunity with that recommendation_id already exists.

Audit trail: Every write-back is logged: what was written, to which CRM object, by which rep, at what time, success/failure. Stored in write_back_log table.

Rollback capability: If a write-back creates something wrong, the admin can see the write-back log and manually delete the CRM record. Automatic rollback is not supported (CRM APIs don’t support transactions).

nodes.title: 4.8 Complete Data Pipeline Flow
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the complete data pipeline flow for processing records from source to platform. It details each step: starting with data ingestion via CSV upload or CRM connector, followed by field mapping to platform-standard names, normalization of data formats, validation of required fields and types, deduplication and merging of records, committing clean data to PostgreSQL tables, enrichment with computed fields, aggregation of statistics, and triggering downstream processes such as cache invalidation and notifications. The document also includes a code snippet illustrating the asynchronous execution of these steps, handling errors via a dead-letter queue, and updating sync cursors for incremental processing.

nodes.title: 4.9 Database Schemas
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the database schema for a core data model, detailing the structure and relationships of several key tables: accounts, contacts, transactions, account_products, and account_enrichment. It specifies fields for each table, including primary keys, foreign keys, and relevant attributes such as company information, contact roles, transaction details, product ownership, and enrichment metrics. The schema also includes audit fields, source system tracking, and JSONB columns for flexible data storage. Additionally, it defines indexes to optimize query performance across tenant, account, and product dimensions.

nodes.title: 4.10 MVP Implementation — CSV Import Flow
nodes.prefix_summary:
## 4.10 MVP Implementation — CSV Import Flow

The MVP experience is deliberately simple. No OAuth, no webhooks, no real-time sync. Just: upload a file, map fields, import.

nodes.title: 4.10.1 MVP Import Types
nodes.summary: This partial document outlines the types of data imports supported in the MVP, detailing three main upload types: Account CSV, Product Catalog CSV, and Transaction History CSV. For each type, it specifies the expected file contents, the database destination and processing engine, and the behavior when files are re-uploaded. All import types use a full replacement strategy, where previous data is soft-deleted or replaced, and relevant enrichment or analysis processes are re-triggered to ensure the system reflects the latest uploaded data.

nodes.title: 4.10.2 MVP Import UX
nodes.summary:
### 4.10.2 MVP Import UX

Step 1: Admin navigates to Settings > Data Import in the Admin Portal.

Step 2: Selects import type (Accounts, Product Catalog, or Transaction History).

Step 3: Drags and drops their CSV/Excel file. System parses header row and shows column preview with sample values.

Step 4: Field mapping screen. Left: detected columns with samples. Right: canonical fields with dropdowns. For first import, admin maps manually. For re-imports, previous mapping is pre-loaded.

Step 5: Click ‘Import.’ System shows progress: ‘Processing... 2,450 / 3,000 records.’

Step 6: Results screen: ‘2,980 records imported successfully. 20 records had issues (view details).’ Failed records shown with error reasons. Admin can download a ‘failed records’ CSV to fix and re-upload.

nodes.title: 4.10.3 CSV Validation Rules
nodes.summary: This partial document outlines the CSV validation rules for file uploads. It specifies constraints such as a maximum file size of 50MB, mandatory header row detection, and required field mappings for different data types (accounts, catalog, transactions). The document details data type validation for dates, numbers, and emails, with error handling for invalid records and incorrect column mappings. It also covers duplicate detection within files, specifying how duplicates are handled and logged. Additionally, it describes encoding detection for various character sets and the fallback process if detection fails. Error handling procedures and user prompts are provided for each validation rule.

nodes.title: 4.11 Nuances, Risks, and Gaps Filled
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines several key gaps, risks, and nuances in the data import process for a platform integrating account, product, and transaction data. Main points covered include: the need for data quality scoring per field and dataset to guide agents and track improvements; the importance of account-to-rep mapping to ensure proper data visibility and scoping; SKU reconciliation to prevent orphaned transactions due to mismatched product identifiers; enforcing correct import order (product catalog before transactions, accounts before transactions) to avoid reference errors; the destructive nature of CSV re-uploads, which replace all data rather than update incrementally; handling CRM API rate limits and using bulk APIs for large data loads; and addressing multi-currency scenarios for global tenants, with normalization or conversion of transaction currencies. The document emphasizes both technical requirements and user experience considerations for robust data integration.

nodes.title: 4.12 Key Technical Decisions Summary
nodes.summary:
This partial document summarizes key technical decisions made for the MVP (Minimum Viable Product) phase of a software project. The main points covered include:

1. **CSV-Only Data Import for MVP:** The MVP will support only CSV/Excel uploads for data import, deferring live CRM connectors to a later phase. This choice avoids complex authentication and integration work, saving significant engineering time.
2. **Pluggable Connector Architecture:** The system will be designed with a connector interface from the start, ensuring future connectors (like Salesforce) can be added without reworking core data processing components.
3. **Full Data Replacement on CSV Re-Upload:** When a CSV is re-uploaded, it will fully replace existing data for that tenant, rather than merging incrementally. This ensures data consistency with the source CRM.
4. **Batch Enrichment Post-Sync:** Data enrichment will be performed as a batch job after data sync, rather than inline during record processing, for efficiency and consistency.
5. **Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) with Configurable Retry:** Error handling will use a DLQ with configurable retries, allowing good records to process while problematic ones are isolated for debugging and potential automatic retry, balancing reliability and visibility.

Overall, the document outlines pragmatic, scalable technical choices to accelerate MVP delivery while preparing for future extensibility.
